exercises.prompt: Which figure of speech is *el río, terco como un viejo*?

options.label: símil
options.feedback: Yes — an explicit comparison with *como*.

options.label: metáfora
options.feedback: Not yet — a metaphor would identify the river with an old man without *como*: *el río, ese viejo terco*.

options.label: hipérbole
options.feedback: Not yet — nothing is exaggerated; two things are compared.

options.label: anáfora
options.feedback: Not yet — anaphora is the repetition of a word at the start of several units.

hints: Look at the little word that links *terco* and *un viejo*.
A comparison with *como* or *cual* has its own name.
exercises.solution: **Símil** (or *comparación*): the river is compared to an old man by means of *como*. A metaphor drops the comparative word and simply identifies one thing with the other: *la luna era una moneda*.

exercises.prompt: *La ciudad dormía con un ojo abierto.* Which figure is this mainly?

options.label: personificación
options.feedback: Yes — the city sleeps and has an eye: human traits given to a place.

options.label: epíteto
options.feedback: Not yet — an epithet is an adjective stating an obvious quality, like *la blanca nieve*.

options.label: antítesis
options.feedback: Not yet — there's a hint of contrast (asleep, eye open), but the main figure gives the city a body and a behaviour.

options.label: paradoja
options.feedback: Not yet — sleeping with one eye open is an everyday idiom, not a contradiction that hides a truth.

hints: Can a city sleep, or have eyes?
The figure gives human qualities to something that isn't human.
exercises.solution: **Personificación** (*prosopopeya*): the city sleeps and keeps one eye open. The phrase also plays on the idiom *dormir con un ojo abierto* — to sleep lightly, on guard.

exercises.prompt:
Undo the *hipérbaton*. Rewrite Bécquer's line in everyday word order, starting with **a colgar**:

*en tu balcón sus nidos a colgar*
answers: a colgar sus nidos en tu balcón
a colgar en tu balcón sus nidos
hints: In neutral order the infinitive comes first, then its direct object, then the place.
*a colgar* + what? + where?
exercises.solution: **a colgar sus nidos en tu balcón.** With the first line, the whole sentence reads *Las oscuras golondrinas volverán a colgar sus nidos en tu balcón*. Restoring the order reveals the periphrasis *volver a* + infinitive: the swallows will hang their nests *again*.

exercises.prompt:
How many metrical syllables does Martí's line have?

*Yo soy un hombre sincero*

options.label: 8 — an octosyllable
options.feedback: Yes — *yo-soy-un-hom-bre-sin-ce-ro*: eight, and *sincero* is *llana*, so the count stands.
Not yet — count again aloud: *yo-soy-un-hom-bre-sin-ce-ro*. No vowels merge here, and the ending needs no adjustment.
Not yet — you would add one only if the last word were *aguda*. *Sincero* is stressed on the penultimate syllable.
Not yet — that is the hendecasyllable of the sonnet; Martí's *Versos sencillos* use a shorter, popular line.

hints: Split it into spoken syllables: *yo-soy-…*
Then look at the stress of *sincero*: last, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable?
exercises.solution: **8.** *Yo-soy-un-hom-bre-sin-ce-ro* gives eight spoken syllables. *Sincero* is *llana*, so no adjustment is made. Octosyllables are the metre of Spanish popular song and ballads — which is why Martí's "simple verses" sound like songs.

exercises.prompt: Darío's line *¡ya te vas para no volver!* has eight spoken syllables. How many syllables does it count **in metre**? Write the number.

feedback.message: Not yet — look at the last word: *volver* is stressed on its final syllable. What does the rule say about *agudo* endings?
Not yet — you subtract one only for an *esdrújula* ending. *Volver* is *aguda*.

hints: Where is the stress in *volver*?
A line ending in an *aguda* word counts one syllable more.
exercises.solution: **9.** *Ya-te-vas-pa-ra-no-vol-ver* = 8 spoken syllables. *Volver* is *aguda*, so we add one: 9. That makes it the same length as the line before it, *Ju-ven-tud-di-vi-no-te-so-ro* (9, *llana*). Both are *eneasílabos*.

exercises.prompt:
How many metrical syllables does the first half of Darío's line have?

*La princesa está triste…*

options.feedback: Yes — *la-prin-ce-sa es-tá-tris-te*, with sinalefa in *sa es*; *triste* is *llana*.
Not yet — you counted *sa* and *es* separately. When a word ends in a vowel and the next begins with one, they usually merge (sinalefa).
Not yet — *triste* is *llana*, so nothing is subtracted.

hints: *princesa* ends in a vowel and *está* begins with one.
Merge them into one syllable, then check the stress of *triste*.
exercises.solution: **7.** *La-prin-ce-sa es-tá-tris-te*: the sinalefa joins *-sa* and *es-* into one syllable. The second half, *qué-ten-drá-la-prin-ce-sa*, also has 7, so the whole line is an *alejandrino* of 14 (7 + 7).

exercises.prompt: What kind of rhyme do *casa* and *alma* make?

options.label: rima asonante
options.feedback: Yes — the vowels match from the stressed vowel (á-a) but the consonants don't (s / lm).

options.label: rima consonante
options.feedback: Not yet — full rhyme needs every sound to match from the stressed vowel, as in *palma / alma*.

options.label: no rhyme at all
options.feedback: Not yet — to a Spanish ear they rhyme: assonance is a real and very common rhyme in Spanish.

hints: Compare everything from the stressed vowel onwards: *-asa* and *-alma*.
The vowels are the same; the consonants are not.
exercises.solution: **Rima asonante.** From the last stressed vowel, *casa* gives á-a and *alma* gives á-a: the vowels match, the consonants don't. Spanish ballads (*romances*) rhyme like this on every even line.

exercises.prompt: What does *¿qué tendrá la princesa?* mean in Darío's line?

options.label: What can be the matter with the princess?
options.feedback: Yes — the future of probability expresses a guess about the present.

options.label: What will the princess have (in the future)?
options.feedback: Not yet — the future here is not about time. It's a guess about her present state.

options.label: What does the princess own?
options.feedback: Not yet — *tener* here is about what is wrong with her (*¿qué tienes?* = what's wrong?), and the future adds conjecture.

options.label: What would the princess have had?
options.feedback: Not yet — that would need a compound conditional; *tendrá* is a simple future.

hints: *¿Qué tienes?* is how Spanish asks 'What's wrong?'
Spanish uses the future to guess about the present: *Serán las diez* = it's probably ten.
exercises.solution: **What can be the matter with the princess?** *¿Qué tiene?* asks what is wrong with someone; putting it in the future (*¿qué tendrá?*) turns it into wondering. The line opens the poem with the speaker's question about her sadness.

exercises.prompt: Give the Spanish term for a line of verse with **eleven** syllables — the line of the sonnet.

feedback.message: Almost — the Spanish spelling has no initial *h*: *endecasílabo*.
Not yet — the *alejandrino* has fourteen syllables. Eleven comes from Greek *hendeka* via Italian.

hints: It starts with the Greek number eleven (*hendeka*), spelled without *h* in Spanish.
endeca- + -sílabo
exercises.solution: **endecasílabo.** It came from Italy in the sixteenth century and became the line of the sonnet and of most serious poetry in Spanish. Bécquer's *Volverán las oscuras golondrinas* is one.

exercises.prompt: In a literary text you read: *Vendieron la casa que **fuera** de su abuelo.* What does *fuera* mean here?

options.label: had been (= había sido)
options.feedback: Yes — in literary and journalistic prose, the *-ra* form can work as a pluperfect indicative, its original Latin meaning.

options.label: might be (a hypothesis)
options.feedback: Not yet — there is nothing hypothetical here; the house really belonged to the grandfather.

options.label: went (from *ir*)
options.feedback: Not yet — *fuera* can come from *ir*, but *la casa que fuera de su abuelo* only makes sense with *ser*.

options.label: outside
options.feedback: Not yet — *fuera* is also an adverb meaning 'outside', but here it is a verb in a relative clause.

hints: There's no *si*, no wish, no doubt: the clause states a fact about the past.
Try replacing *fuera* with *había sido*.
exercises.solution: **had been.** *La casa que fuera de su abuelo* = *la casa que había sido de su abuelo*. The *-ra* form descends from the Latin pluperfect indicative, and literary and journalistic Spanish still uses it that way: *el que fuera presidente* — the former president.

exercises.prompt: Which **two** figures appear in *Juventud, divino tesoro, / ¡ya te vas para no volver!*? Select both.

options.label: apóstrofe
options.feedback: Yes — the speaker addresses youth directly, as if it could hear (*te vas*).

options.label: metáfora
options.feedback: Yes — youth is called a *divino tesoro* without any *como*.

options.label: símil
options.feedback: Not yet — there is no comparative word like *como*; youth simply *is* a treasure.

options.label: hipérbaton
options.feedback: Not yet — the word order here is quite natural.

hints: Who is the speaker talking to?
What is youth called, and is there a *como*?
exercises.solution: **Apóstrofe and metáfora.** The speaker turns to youth and speaks to it in the second person (*te vas*) — an apostrophe. Calling it *divino tesoro* identifies it with a treasure — a metaphor. The personification of youth as someone leaving runs underneath both.
